chapter: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
title: Claude Jones as his inspiration, and Lawrence Brown's later influence
summary: Claude Jones talked him into trombone and was his model; Dickie Wells seemed too complicated, and Lawrence Brown influenced everyone after 1932.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: Well, Claude Jones really influenced me.

He talked me into, really talked me into playing trombone. I didn't have no idea of ever playing a trombone before, and if you listen to Claude Jones anyway, Claude Jones could talk you into anything, if you knew Claude, --

-- see? And Claude really -- he got me interested. He got me interested in the trombone. And listening to him play with McKinney Cottonpickers, I thought there was nobody in the world but Claude Jones.

I had heard Dickie Wells play with Lloyd Scott at home around that same time, you know, during the same time, 1926 and '27 and '28. But Dickie's style was so complicated to me that it didn't impress me like Claude did. It was interesting to listen to him but Claude, you see, Claude could play melodies and his jazz playing was sensible. It was intricate, too, at the same time. If you listen to early
McKinney Cottonpicker records that was made in 1928, back in there, and '29, you would hear this.
Then, after that, when Lawrence Brown came to New York in '32, Lawrence Brown started to influence a lot of trombone players and he influenced me too, you see.
And he had everybody trying to play his solo on the 'Sheik.'
That's the record he made with Duke, you know, and 'Ducky-Wucky' and all those things.
So, really, my inspiration really was Claude Jones from the beginning.
